## Question

Assuming the latest Docker with BuildKit enabled, the [documentation](https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/commandline/buildx_build/#secret) suggests that the `--secret` option has `file` and `env` types. I want to use the `env` type like this:

```
MYSECRET=thepassword
docker build --secret id=mysecret,env=MYSECRET -t myimage .
```

In the dockerfile, the secret would be accessed like:

```
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=mysecret \
    PASSWORD=$(cat /run/secrets/mysecret) && \
    <run command taking password arg> ${PASSWORD}
```

This approach fails with `cat: /run/secrets/mysecret: No such file or directory`

A similar issue was asked [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/71771929/how-can-i-read-secret-args-passed-to-docker-build-as-environment-variables-to) but the extra steps writing the secrets into the .condarc file inside the docker image aren't important to me. According to that post, the basic operation of getting a local environment var passed into the docker build for the scope of a single RUN statement should "work", but it doesn't for me.

The build command above runs fine until it tries to access the file path that is supposed to be mapped to the secret. Trying temporarily to pass MYSECRET into the build as a --build-arg shows that the env var can be resolved.

T…

The current landscape of actively supported major versions includes: Note: Older versions like 13 and below are officially end-of-life and no longer receive community security updates.

PostgreSQL uses a Major.Minor versioning format. Major versions introduce new features, while minor versions provide security patches and bug fixes. The PostgreSQL community officially supports a major version for 5 years from its release date.

Minor releases are scheduled at least once per quarter, usually in February, May, August, and November, with additional unscheduled releases possible when critical security or stability issues need faster attention. At the end of the five-year support period, a PostgreSQL major version reaches end-of-life, or EOL. Once a version is EOL, it no longer receives security patches, bug fixes, or maintenance updates. For this reason, organizations should begin upgrade planning well before the EOL date rather than waiting until support has already ended.

query: We are moving to the newest Go release — which language or standard library changes could break working code, and which of them can be reverted with a GODEBUG setting?

page.title: Go, Backwards Compatibility, and GODEBUG - The Go Programming Language
page.content:
When preparing any change that is permitted by Go 1 compatibility but may nonetheless break some existing programs, we first engineer the change to keep as many existing programs working as possible. For the remaining programs, we define a new GODEBUG setting that allows individual programs to opt back in to the old behavior. A GODEBUG setting may not be added if doing so is infeasible, but that should be extremely rare. GODEBUG settings added for compatibility will be maintained for a minimum of two years (four Go releases).

There are, however, times when we cannot maintain complete compatibility. If code depends on buggy (including insecure) behavior, then fixing the bug will break that code. New features can also have similar impacts: enabling the HTTP/2 use by the HTTP client broke programs connecting to servers with buggy HTTP/2 implementations. These kinds of changes are unavoidable and permitted by the Go 1 compatibility rules. Even so, Go provides a mechanism called GODEBUG to reduce the impact such changes have on Go developers using newer toolchains to compile old code.

Mauna Loa Observatory - NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory

The 2022 eruption of the Mauna Loa volcano cut off road access to the Mauna Loa Baseline Observatory. Construction on the temporary Mauna Loa Access road was completed on 26 March, 2026.

At this time, there is no site access for the general public to the Mauna Loa Observatory and NOAA has not yet established a public opening date. GML and scientific partners are working together to bring mission critical scientific projects back online. It is still unclear when utility infrastructure will be replaced and power re-established to the site.

We will provide another update as more information becomes available.

Media contact: Theo Stein at (303) 819-7409 or theo.stein@noaa.gov.

# NOAA In Situ Carbon Dioxide (CO2) Measurements

## Organization(s):

National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Global Monitoring Laboratory (GML)

## What does this program measure?

Carbon Dioxide (CO2) is measured in parts-per-million (ppm) and reported in units of micromol mol-1 (10-6 mol CO2 per mol of dry air). Measurements are directly traceable to the WMO CO2 mole fraction scale.

## How does this program work?

Carbon dioxide (CO2) in ambient and standard air samples is detected using a non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) analyzer. The measurement of CO2 in air is made relative to reference standards whose CO2 mixing ratio is determined with high precision and accuracy. Ambient air samples are bracketed by a pair of reference standards every hour to correct for non-linearity in detector response.

## How to Write a Refund Policy Customers Actually Trust

A refund policy is one of the highest-traffic pages on most e-commerce sites and one of the least considered. Customers read it before they buy, not after, and a vague one costs you the sale.

Start with the window. Thirty days is the default customers expect; anything shorter needs a reason stated on the page. Say when the clock starts — delivery date, not order date, unless you have a reason to differ.

Be explicit about condition. "Unused and in original packaging" means something; "in resalable condition" invites an argument. Photographs help on both sides.

Name who pays return shipping. This is the single most disputed line in any refund policy. If the customer pays, say so in the first paragraph, not in a footnote. If you pay for defective items only, define defective.

Set the refund timeline honestly. "Within five business days of receiving the return" is a promise you can keep. "Immediately" is not.

Cover exchanges separately. Many customers want a different size, not their money back, and burying exchanges inside the refund policy sends them to a competitor.

Write it in plain sentences. Legal-sounding boilerplate reads as evasive, and the whole purpose of the page is to make a nervous buyer comfortable enough to check out.

Finally, link it from the product page and the cart, not just the footer. A policy nobody finds does none of this work.

## Nine Rules for Slides That Don't Lose the Room

One idea per slide. If you need a second sentence to explain why the chart is there, it belongs on its own slide or in the appendix.

Put the takeaway in the title. "Q3 Revenue by Region" tells the audience nothing. "Revenue growth is coming entirely from EMEA" tells them what to look at and why.

Kill the bullet nest. Sub-bullets under sub-bullets are a sign the thinking is not finished. Flatten to three points or split the slide.

Size type for the back row. Twenty-four point is the practical floor for body text in a conference room, and most decks violate it by slide four.

Use one accent colour. Decks that colour every series differently force the audience to consult a legend instead of reading the shape of the data.

Label directly. A line labelled at its right end beats a legend every time, because the eye never has to leave the chart.

Cut the logo from every slide. It appears on the title slide; after that it is spending attention you need elsewhere.

Build complex charts in stages. Show the baseline, then the change, then the conclusion, on three clicks rather than all at once.

Rehearse the transitions, not the words. Audiences forgive imperfect phrasing and never forgive a presenter fumbling for the next slide.
